subject: Career
title: Internal Equity: What Peers Earn
description: A quick, practical guide to Internal Equity: What Peers Earn.

hook.text: You discover a colleague with the same title earns 20% more. Suddenly, your salary feels unfair.

buildup.text: Internal equity means fair pay among employees doing similar work. Many companies fail at it.

discovery.text: Pay compression happens when new hires get market rates while tenured employees stagnate.

twist.text: Companies fear the domino effect — fix one salary and everyone else asks. So they avoid it.

climax.text: Bringing market data and peer comparisons to a raise conversation is more effective than emotions.

punchline.text: Fairness doesn't fix itself. You have to ask.

quiz.question: What is pay compression?
options: New hires earning as much as tenured employees

details.summary: Internal equity refers to how your pay compares to colleagues in similar roles within the same organization. Understanding internal pay structures helps you identify whether you are compensated fairly and provides data for evidence-based raise conversations.
details.whyItMatters: Internal pay gaps breed resentment and attrition. Employees who discover and address inequities early protect both their earnings and their workplace morale.
takeaways: Internal equity data is powerful ammunition in raise discussions
Pay transparency laws are making internal gaps more visible
Approach peer pay conversations with discretion and professionalism

faq.question: Is it appropriate to ask coworkers about their salaries?
faq.answer: In most jurisdictions it is legally protected to discuss pay with coworkers. Approach the conversation privately and with genuine curiosity rather than competition. Framing it as mutual information sharing creates trust and produces more honest answers.

faq.question: What should I do if I discover a significant internal pay gap?
faq.answer: Document the discrepancy with objective data including role scope, tenure, and performance metrics. Present the case to your manager or HR as a market alignment request rather than a complaint. Focus on data-driven fairness rather than emotional arguments.
